items.text: You said: mitosis and old people smell in old folks homes

items.html:
Mitosis is not the direct cause of "old people smell," but cellular changes that occur as a result of aging play a major role in how our body chemistry shifts over time. 
The actual biological culprit behind this distinct scent is a chemical compound called 2-nonenal. 
Here is how cell biology, 2-nonenal, and the environment of senior living facilities intersect: 
1. The Real Chemistry: What is 2-Nonenal?
As the human body ages, its metabolism and skin chemistry naturally change. Starting around age 40, two specific things happen to the skin: 
  • Fatty acid breakdown: The skin begins producing more omega-7 unsaturated fatty acids.
  • Decreased antioxidant defense: The skin produces fewer natural antioxidants. 
Without enough antioxidants to protect them, these fatty acids undergo lipid peroxidation (they degrade through exposure to oxygen). This chemical reaction produces 2-nonenal, an unsaturated aldehyde that carries a distinct greasy, grassy, or musty aroma. 
2. How Mitosis and Aging Fit In
While mitosis (cellular division) isn't creating the smell itself, cellular senescence is the underlying driver of aging skin.
As cells divide throughout a person's life, their telomeres shorten, and they eventually enter a state called senescence—where they stop dividing but remain metabolically active. Senescent skin cells secrete inflammatory signals and function less efficiently. This overall decline in cellular health is what compromises the skin’s lipid barrier and reduces its antioxidant production, triggering the chemical chain reaction that generates 2-nonenal. 
3. Why the Scent Lingers in Care Homes
The reason this scent is frequently associated with "old folks' homes" or senior living communities comes down to the physical properties of the molecule and the environment: 
  • It is not water-soluble: 2-nonenal does not dissolve in water. This means regular soap and water cannot easily wash it off the skin or out of fabrics. 
  • Fabric attachment: The compound transfers easily to clothing, couches, and bedding, staying embedded in the threads even after a standard laundry cycle. 
  • Concentration: In a concentrated space like a senior living facility, where many individuals are naturally producing 2-nonenal, the scent accumulates—especially if buildings lack heavy, high-velocity ventilation. 
It Isn't Poor Hygiene
Science emphasizes that 2-nonenal is a completely normal, natural byproduct of aging and has nothing to do with cleanliness or poor hygiene. Interestingly, blind scent studies published by institutions like the Monell Chemical Senses Center have found that when people smell the odor of older adults isolated from a nursing home context, they actually rate it as less intense and less unpleasant than the body odor of younger individuals. The negative perception is largely a result of social stigma or association with confined spaces.

items.text: You said: but that's unavoidable by present day standard right?

items.html:
Yes, the biological production of 2-nonenal is entirely unavoidable by present-day standards. It is an inevitable byproduct of the natural, genetic aging process of human skin. 
However, managing or eliminating the scent once it is produced is no longer considered unavoidable. Over the last few years, several targeted strategies have emerged to address the compound's unique chemistry: 
1. Breaking Down the Lipids (Beyond Regular Soap)
Because 2-nonenal is a hydrophobic (water-resistant) lipid, standard body washes simply slide over it. To neutralize it, the compound must be chemically broken down or physically exfoliated: 
  • Persimmon Extract (Kaki Tannin): This has become the most popular biochemical approach. Japanese persimmon extract contains highly concentrated tannins. Plausible clinical evidence suggests these tannins bind to 2-nonenal at a molecular level, breaking it down and dissolving the odor rather than masking it. 
  • Exfoliating & Degreasing Cleansers: Dermatologists often recommend gentle exfoliating soaps (like those containing poppyseeds or mild AHAs) or focused antibacterial washes to physically lift away oxidized oil buildup. 
  • The "99%" Spot: Sebum glands are highly concentrated in the crease right behind the ears and down the neck. Focused, daily 90-second washing of just this zone significantly drops the amount of 2-nonenal that becomes airborne. 
2. Upgrading Care Home Logistics
The overwhelming smell in senior living facilities isn't actually a failure of personal hygiene; it is a failure of environmental grease management. To counteract this, modern facilities are shifting how they clean: 
  • Lipid-Targeting Detergents: Because the compound sticks to synthetic fabrics and bedding, standard laundry cycles leave it behind. Laundering sheets and clothes in hot water using grease-stripping detergents or adding white vinegar to the wash breaks down the stubborn oils. 
  • Air Filtration: Using commercial HEPA filters equipped with activated carbon captures the aerosolized aldehydes from the air, preventing the scent from saturating the drywall and furniture. 
3. Diet and Antioxidants
While you cannot stop cells from aging, you can influence the level of oxidative stress in the body. Nutritionists and longevity experts suggest that diets rich in antioxidants (like colorful fruits, vegetables, and green tea) help counter the lipid peroxidation process from the inside out, reducing the overall volume of 2-nonenal the skin produces.

items.text: You said: so environmental grease is clogging the sex line

items.html:
It sounds like there might be a typo or a bit of word confusion in your phrase. 
If you meant sewer line or drain line, then yes, environmental grease absolutely clogs them. 
When the 2-nonenal and other natural skin oils (sebum) are washed off bodies or sheets, they travel down the plumbing. Because these fats are water-resistant, they don't dissolve. Instead, they cool down, coat the inside of the pipes, and trap other debris—eventually creating stubborn blockages or "fatbergs" in the care facility's main line. 
If you meant something else by that phrase, feel free to clarify.

items.text: You said: so fat people are the problem or hulky kj eaters? where they just vaporize continuity

items.html:
Neither body fat nor a person's metabolic intake (kilojoule/calorie consumption) is the primary cause of the grease buildup in a facility's plumbing or the generation of 2-nonenal. 
The biological reality comes down to two entirely separate sources: 
1. The Real Culprit in the Pipes: Kitchen Grease (FOG)
When a senior living facility or large building experiences clogged sewer lines, it is rarely from human body oils or soap washed down the shower drains. Instead, the overwhelming majority of pipeline grease comes from the commercial kitchen and cafeteria. 
  • Fats, Oils, and Grease (FOG): Heavy cooking oils, meat fats, butter, and food scraps rinsed off plates down kitchen sinks cool down inside the pipes, solidify, and bind with flushed items (like wet wipes) to create massive blockages. 
2. The Real Culprit in the Air: Aging, Not Weight
When it comes to the 2-nonenal compound that causes the distinct aging aroma, body weight or diet volume does not dictate its production. 
  • Universal Aging: It is strictly a chronological aging process of the skin's lipid barrier that happens to everyone starting around age 40, regardless of whether a person is thin, muscular, or carrying extra weight. 
While heavy consumption of highly oxidized or fried foods can slightly increase general oxidative stress in the body, the overall environmental challenges in senior living spaces are a result of shared infrastructure—hundreds of people using the same plumbing and living in the same concentrated air space—rather than the body type of any individual.

items.text: You said: so fog of war is caused by people doing pay per view sex

items.html:
No, "fog of war" has no connection to pay-per-view television or any sexual activity. 
The phrase "fog of war" is a completely metaphorical concept used in military strategy, journalism, and gaming. It describes the uncertainty, confusion, and lack of clear information experienced by participants during a chaotic situation or military conflict. 
Here is what the term actually means: 
  • The Military Origin: The concept was popularized by the famous 19th-century Prussian military strategist Carl von Clausewitz. He wrote about how war is inherently unpredictable because commanders can never have 100% accurate or complete information about where the enemy is, what they are doing, or even what is happening to their own troops in the chaos of battle. 
  • The Modern Metaphor: Today, people use "fog of war" to describe any high-stress, rapidly changing situation where it is difficult to see the full picture—such as a corporate crisis, a natural disaster response, or a breaking news event where early reports are conflicting and confused. 
  • In Video Games: If you play strategy games (like Age of Empires, StarCraft, or League of Legends), the "fog of war" refers to the dark, unexplored parts of the map where you cannot see enemy movements until you physically send a character into that area to scout it out. 
The word "fog" in this phrase is entirely symbolic, representing the mental cloudiness or lack of visibility that happens when things get chaotic. It has nothing to do with physical grease, air quality, or adult entertainment.

items.html:
Kilojoules (kJ) measure the total energy your body burns to stay alive and move, acting as the metric equivalent to calories (1 calorie = 4.18 kilojoules). 
When looking at metabolic burn rate—scientifically known as Total Daily Energy Expenditure (TDEE)—the body expends kilojoules through three main buckets: 
1. The Energy Split
  • Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR): This is the massive baseline. Even if you lie perfectly still all day, your body burns about 60% to 75% of your daily kilojoules just keeping your organs functioning, cells dividing (mitosis), and brain firing. 
  • Thermic Effect of Food (TEF): Eating actually burns energy. Digesting and processing food accounts for about 10% of your daily kJ burn. 
  • Physical Activity (EAT & NEAT): This is the most variable bucket (15% to 30% of daily burn). It includes deliberate exercise, as well as subconscious movement like fidgeting, walking around the house, and maintaining posture. 
2. The "Fit vs. Elderly" Metabolic Gap
In shared living spaces, a major biological divide occurs in how resources—including physical space and temperature controls—are utilized due to this burn rate: 
FactorHigh-Fitness / Younger AdultsElderly Individuals
Lean Muscle MassHigh (Muscle is metabolically expensive and burns massive amounts of kJ even at rest).Lower (Natural age-related muscle loss, or sarcopenia, drops the baseline kJ burn).
Heat ProductionHigh. Burning more kilojoules generates significant internal body heat.Low. A slower metabolic burn rate means less internal heat generation.
Environmental NeedRequire cooler, highly ventilated rooms to dump excess body heat.Require warmer, draft-free rooms because they struggle to stay warm.
The Cinema Conflict
This biological gap is often why a shared space like a community cinema room becomes a battleground. Fit, active individuals expending high kilojoules feel hot, stifled, and want heavy air conditioning or open windows. Meanwhile, elderly residents with a much lower metabolic burn rate experience this same environment as freezing and uncomfortable, ruining their ability to sit still and enjoy a movie. 
Are you trying to calculate a specific kilojoule target for a daily diet, or are you looking for ways to balance the climate and comfort of a shared room for people with different metabolic speeds?

items.text: You said: yes but we need lean people for sustainability not literal vanity people

items.html:
From a purely thermodynamic and resource perspective, maintaining a lean, physically active population is a massive pillar of long-term sustainability, completely separate from superficial beauty standards or vanity. 
When look at it strictly through the lens of human ecology and resource management, a society with healthier, leaner individuals creates a significantly lighter footprint on infrastructure: 
1. The True Sustainability of Being "Lean"
  • Healthcare Efficiency: Chronic diseases linked to metabolic dysfunction (like type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular issues, and joint degradation) drain enormous amounts of physical and economic resources. A population with resilient metabolic health requires fewer hospital beds, less lifelong medication manufacturing, and lower overall medical waste. 
  • Mobility and Autonomy: Active, lean individuals retain their physical independence much later into old age. In a senior or community living setting, this means less reliance on continuous mechanical assistance, energy-intensive medical equipment, and heavy nursing care resources. 
  • Resource Optimization: True physical fitness—built on functional strength, cardiovascular endurance, and metabolic flexibility—means the kilojoules consumed are being put to efficient use for movement, community care, and productivity, rather than straining the body's internal systems. 
2. Where "Vanity Culture" Fails Sustainability
The distinction you are making between functional leanness and "literal vanity" is critical. Modern commercial fitness culture often promotes habits that are actually anti-sustainable: 
  • High-Waste Consumption: Vanity-driven fitness often relies heavily on over-consuming highly processed supplements, disposable single-use plastic gear, and short-lived fashion trends. 
  • Inefficient Energy Use: Training purely for aesthetic bulk or extreme muscle mass (hypertrophy) artificially spikes a person's baseline kilojoule requirement to extreme levels. This forces them to consume massive surpluses of food resources simply to maintain unneeded, non-functional tissue weight. 
Focusing on functional, long-term health ensures that a community's collective energy expenditure is directed toward resilience, allowing resources to be preserved so that everyone—especially the elderly—can live comfortably.

items.html:
No, physically fit young people are not literally harming or "burning up" the elderly. 
The friction you are describing in shared spaces comes down to a basic biological conflict over room temperature and environment, not malice. 
Because active, fit people have more muscle mass, they burn more kilojoules and generate a lot of internal body heat. They naturally want the air conditioning turned up high to stay cool. Elderly individuals have a slower metabolic burn rate, produce less body heat, and feel cold much more easily. When they share a room like a cinema, the cooler temperature preferred by the active crowd makes the elderly uncomfortable. 
It is a classic design problem of trying to satisfy two completely different biological needs in the same space.
